sections.body:
A pump moves water. The water comes from a well, a sump or a tank, and a motor turns an impeller that pushes the water up a pipe. Two arrangements are common. In the first, the motor sits above the water on a frame, and the pump lifts the water up to it. In the second, the motor is sealed inside a case that is lowered into the water and stays there. This is a submersible pump, and the case, the cable and the water all meet in the same place.

Five words carry the subject. Current is the flow of electricity, measured in amperes (A). Insulation is the material around the live part of the cable that keeps the current inside it. The earth is the ground itself, and the earth conductor is the green-and-yellow wire that joins the metal parts of the installation to it. Leakage current is the small current that always escapes through the insulation, and it grows when the insulation is damaged. And water with minerals in it carries current: pure water is a poor conductor, but the water in a well, a sump or a tank is not pure water.

The fault is simple to state. If the live part of the cable or of the motor touches the water, current can leave the cable, cross into the water, reach the ground and reach a person who is standing on wet ground or holding a metal pipe. Nothing about the pump looks wrong from the outside. The fault is inside the cable or inside the case, and it is done to a person who is standing in the water.

This article explains where the leakage comes from, what protects the circuit, how to check an installation, and what to do in the first minutes after a shock. It does not replace the manual of the pump, and it does not replace the work of a licensed electrician.
examples: A submersible pump sits in the water, so its case and its cable are in the same place as the water.
Current leaves the cable only when the insulation is broken, and the water carries it from there.
The manual and the electrician decide what is done; this article explains the risk.
sections.heading: What a pump is, and why the water meets the current

terms.example: The current went back through the earth conductor instead of through the motor.
terms.gloss: The flow of electricity, measured in amperes (A).

terms.example: The pump in the sump moves the water up into the tank.
terms.gloss: A machine that moves water from one place to another.

terms.example: A submersible pump hangs on a cable inside the well.
terms.gloss: A pump whose motor is sealed in a case that works under water.

terms.example: The insulation on the cable is cracked where it passes over the edge of the pit.
terms.gloss: The material around the live part of a cable that keeps the current inside it.

terms.example: The electrician measured the leakage current before he ran the pump again.
terms.gloss: Current that escapes from the live part of a cable or a pump through damaged insulation.

sections.body:
Leakage current starts at a place where the insulation is not what it should be. A cable runs from the board to the pump, and it is the most exposed part of the installation: it lies on the floor of a pit, along the wall of a well, or over the edge of a tank. It can be cracked by age, pinched where it passes over a sharp edge of the well or of the pit, cut by a tool during other work, or chewed by a rodent. Any of these opens a path from the live conductor to the outside of the cable, and the outside of the cable is under water.

The other entry point is the pump itself. The motor has a terminal box: the small box on the cable side that holds the connections between the cable and the motor. Its lid seals against the water, and the seal and the glands that hold the cable are what keep the water out. A lid that is not closed properly, a gland that is loose, or a terminal box that is not the type for the pump lets the water in. When there is water in the terminal box, the current can start inside the pump.

The third way is a missing or a broken earth. A pump with no earth conductor has no safe way for a fault current to go back to the board. It can be a supply cable with no earth conductor at all, a pump fed from a generator or from an extension lead that has no earth, a tank or a metal pipework that is not earthed, or an earth conductor that has been cut, for example by a drill during a renovation. In every case the result is the same: when a fault happens, the current looks for another path, and the wet ground is there.
examples: The cable lies on the floor of the pit, and that is where it gets damaged.
Water in the terminal box means the current can start inside the pump.
The installation had no earth conductor at all, so there was no safe way back for a fault current.
sections.heading: Where the leakage comes from

terms.example: The pump hangs ten metres down inside the well.
terms.gloss: A deep hole dug in the ground that holds the water a pump lifts.

terms.example: The sump in the basement pit fills when the floor drain backs up.
terms.gloss: A pit that collects water from a floor or a basement so that a pump can lift it.

terms.example: The earth conductor was cut by a drill during the renovation.
terms.gloss: The green-and-yellow wire that connects the metal parts of an installation to the earth.

sections.body:
Current does not travel alone. It needs a closed path: it leaves the board on the live conductor and comes back on the neutral conductor, and it will take any path that closes the loop. If the live part of the pump touches the water, the water becomes part of that loop. The ground becomes part of it too, because the water in a well or in a tank is in contact with the ground.

So the paths that can carry current are worth naming: the wet ground around a pump, a concrete floor that is wet, the metal pipework and the water in the tank, the metal lid of the pit, and a cable whose insulation has failed. Each one of them on its own is harmless. A person, a wet floor and a live pump together are the fault.

Your body becomes part of the circuit the moment it touches two points at different voltages. While you stand on wet ground and hold a metal pipe, current passes through you instead of through the earth conductor that was meant to carry it safely. The severity is not decided by the voltage alone. It is decided by the path the current takes through the body and by how long the current flows. The supply to a house is around 230 V in much of the world and around 120 V in North America, and those voltages are enough to move current through a person whenever the path is short and the ground is wet. A current that a person can feel is already a reason to stop, because a muscle that contracts by itself may not let go: the hand stays on the pipe.

Earthing is the arrangement that gives a fault current a low-resistance way back to the board instead of through the person. Where it is missing, the current takes the path that is left. This is why the first rule after a shock is to break the circuit, and not to pull the person away.
examples: The water in the tank is in contact with the ground, so the ground is part of the circuit.
The severity depends on the path through the body and on the time, not on the voltage alone.
A hand that grips a pipe does not let go by itself; break the circuit first.
sections.heading: The path back to the person

terms.example: The earthing of the pump was checked when the board was replaced.
terms.gloss: The whole arrangement that connects the metal parts of an installation to the earth, so that a fault current has a safe way back.

sections.body:
Six parts guard a pump installation, and they watch different things. The earth conductor, the residual-current device and the circuit breaker watch the electricity. The ingress protection rating, the float switch and the dry-run protection watch the pump and the water around it. A reader who mixes the two groups will wait for the wrong part to save them.

The ratings in the table are the common levels, not the law. A residual current of 30 mA is the usual level for personal protection in most installations, and a submersible pump is often marked IP68. The local standard decides every one of these values. If the installation in front of you does not match the table, ask the electrician or the utility what it should be.

One rating is worth reading on the nameplate before anything else: the ingress protection rating. It says how well the casing of the motor keeps out water and solid objects, and a pump that is marked for immersion is marked for it. It is not a permission to lift the pump out of the water and run it there.
examples: The earth conductor, the residual-current device and the breaker watch the current; the rating, the float switch and the dry-run protection watch the pump.
The residual-current device trips when the current that comes back is smaller than the current that went out.
Thirty milliamps is the typical level for personal protection in most installations, and the local standard decides.
sections.heading: The protection, and what each one does

headers: What it does when it works
What it does not protect against
rows: Protective earth conductor
It watches the connection between the live part and the metal parts of the installation.
It carries the fault current back to the board, so that the breaker opens.
No rating; it is a continuous conductor, and the local standard decides its size.
It does nothing at all if it has been cut, and it does not protect a person who is already in the water.
Residual-current device (RCD)
It watches the difference between the current that leaves the circuit and the current that returns.
It trips and cuts the power in a fraction of a second when the two currents differ.
Typically 30 mA for personal protection in most installations; the local standard decides.
It does not protect against an overload, where the current goes out and comes back the normal way.
Circuit breaker
It watches the current in the circuit against the rating of the cable.
It opens the circuit when the current is too high, so that the cable cannot overheat.
A common rating for a socket circuit is 16 A, and a pump is often on a circuit of its own; the local standard decides.
It does not protect a person from a small leakage current; only the residual-current device does that.
Ingress protection rating of the pump
It watches the seal of the casing of the motor against water and solid objects.
It tells the reader that the casing is built to work under water, so the pump can stay submerged.
A submersible pump is often marked IP68; the maker states the depth and the time, and the local standard decides the installation.
It does not protect the cable, the plug or the socket, and it is no permission to run the pump dry.
Float switch
It watches the water level in the tank or in the pit.
It starts the pump when the level rises and stops it when the level falls.
A switch on a float, set to the level of the tank; the maker and the local standard decide the setting.
It does not protect the cable or the person, and a switch set at the wrong level does not protect the motor.
Dry-run protection
It watches whether there is water around the motor, by the current the motor draws or by the heat in the motor.
It stops the pump when the pump turns without water, so that the motor is not damaged.
Often built into the pump or added as a separate device; the maker and the local standard decide.
It does not protect the cable, the socket or the person, and it does not find a fault in the insulation.

terms.example: The residual-current device is the wide switch on the board with the test button.
terms.gloss: A device that compares the current going out with the current coming back, and opens the circuit when they differ.

terms.example: The nameplate of this pump carries an ingress protection rating of IP68.
terms.gloss: The IP code on the nameplate that says how well the casing keeps out solid objects and water.

terms.example: The float switch in the tank stops the pump when the tank is empty.
terms.gloss: A switch on a float that starts or stops the pump when the water level rises or falls.

sections.body:
A pump installation can be checked by the person who looks after it, and the check takes a few minutes. Nothing in the routine touches the wiring, and nothing in it opens the pump. If a step shows a fault, the answer is to switch off, report it and call a licensed electrician: the routine is for finding out that something is wrong, not for fixing it.

The order matters, because the first steps establish that the pump is in a safe state to look at, and the later steps look at the parts that carry current. The test button on the residual-current device is the check that the protection is still alive: if the device does not trip when you press it, the device is not protecting anything, whatever the pump is doing.

Two faults are worth naming here. A dry run happens when the pump turns with no water around the motor; in a submersible pump the water is what cools the motor, and a dry run heats it. Backflow is water moving in the wrong direction, back along the pipe towards the pump: in some installations the water that runs back leaves the pump running with nothing to move, and that is a dry run again.
examples: The pump is on its own circuit, and the residual-current device is the wide switch with the test button.
I stopped at the first crack in the cable, near the edge of the pit.
The socket is above the pit, and it stays dry.
sections.heading: A safe check routine for a pump installation
steps: Know which supply the pump is on, and confirm that the pump has a circuit of its own and that the circuit is protected by a residual-current device.
Test the residual-current device with its test button, and confirm that it trips and resets.
Look at the cable along its whole length, from the plug to the pump, and stop at the first crack, cut or pinch you find.
Keep a submersible pump under water while it runs, and keep the lid of the pit closed.
Never run the pump dry: check that the level, the float switch and the tank are in order before you start it.
Keep the socket, the plug and the connection above the pit out of the water, and keep them dry.

terms.example: A dry run heats the motor of a submersible pump.
terms.gloss: The pump turning without water around it, so that the motor has nothing to cool it.

terms.example: After the supply stops, backflow can leave the pump running with no water.
terms.gloss: Water moving in the wrong direction, back along the pipe towards the pump.

sections.body:
Never work on the pump with the power on. Not the cable, not the terminal box, not the plug, and not with the breaker switched off and the hope that it was already off. If you cannot confirm that the circuit is dead, you do not work on it.

Never pull the pump out of the water by its cable. The cable is not a handle. It carries the weight of the pump, and a pump that is not fixed to a bracket can pull the cable down on the edge of the pit or over a pulley, cut it, and go out of control. Use the chain, the rope or the bracket that the maker supplies.

Never run a submersible pump dry. The motor of a submersible pump is cooled by the water around it. Run it with no water and the motor has no cooling at all, and it can be damaged in a short time. If the level is low or the tank is empty, the pump waits.

Never connect the pump to a generator or to an extension lead that has no earth. A generator and a lead without an earth conductor remove the safe path back to the supply, so a fault current looks for another path, and the wet ground is there. Where the pump needs a supply that the building does not have, the answer is a circuit fitted by an electrician.

Never reset the residual-current device again and again instead of finding the fault. A device that trips has found a fault. Resetting it clears the evidence and puts the fault back. Note what the pump was doing, note the time, and call the electrician. A device that trips twice in one week is a fault to be reported, not a nuisance to be pushed.

And one rule above the five: **only a licensed electrician opens, repairs or tests the installation.** The manual of the pump, the local standard and the certificate of the electrician decide what is done. This article explains what happens and what to do in the first minutes. It is not a repair instruction, and it does not replace any of those three.
examples: I will not pull the pump out by the cable; I will use the chain that the maker supplied.
The residual-current device has tripped twice, so it will not be reset again; the fault has to be found.
Only a licensed electrician opens the installation, so I will call one and keep the pump out of service.
sections.heading: Five things never to do

sections.body:
Most of what you need in this job is the language of a report and of a request. Say what you saw, say what the device did, and say what you want done next. Do not diagnose the fault yourself; describe the symptom and let the electrician decide the cause.

A technician needs four things: where the pump is, what the nameplate says, the symptom in the order it happened, and what has already been tried. Read the nameplate before you call, and keep it in front of you when the technician arrives. A landlord or an office manager needs the same facts in a shorter form, plus the request: a date, a reference number and the statement that the pump is out of service. A colleague needs the rule and the warning: switch off, call, do not reset.
examples: The pump in the basement sump is out of service, and the residual-current device has tripped twice.
The nameplate gives the make, the model and the ingress protection rating, and I have written them down.
Somebody got a shock from the pump while they were standing in the water; I have switched off the power at the board.
Could you send a licensed electrician and give me a reference number for the visit?
The pump stays out of service until the earth connection and the cable have been checked.
I do not know what caused it; I can tell you exactly what I saw and in which order it happened.
Do not reset the device again. Call the utility and let them find the fault.
Is the service of the pump included in the lease, or do I have to arrange it?
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
A shock in the water is an emergency, and the first minutes decide the result. The order below matters. Do not start with the person; start with the power. A person standing in the water is still part of the circuit, and your hand on their arm makes you part of it too.

Switch off the power at the breaker or at the main switch if you can reach it without entering the wet area. If you cannot reach it safely, do not go into the water. Move everybody out, call the emergency number and wait for the power to be cut from a safe position. Then dry the person and the floor, especially the hands and the feet, and dry the pit and the ground around the pump. Do not touch a switch or a socket in the wet area: you cannot be sure that the earth path is working, and this is the moment not to test it.

Call the emergency number if the person is not responding, or if you are not sure how serious it is. In Vietnam the ambulance is 115 and the police and the traffic service are 113; in much of Europe it is 112; in the United Kingdom it is 999; and in the United States and Canada it is 911. Say where you are, what happened, and what the person is doing now. After that, call the electrician and the utility, keep the pump out of service until it has been checked, and write down the time of the event, the symptoms and the names of the people you called.

Then think about who is responsible, because it decides who has to act. The installer who built the installation is responsible for the work: the earth conductor, the protection and the circuit are his until he has certified them. The owner, the landlord or the office manager who keeps the building, is responsible for the upkeep: the checks, the repairs, the service and the access to the pump. The utility is responsible for the supply: the meter, the main switch and the service line. Where the installation is old, the responsibility can be unclear, and that is a question for the utility and for the local authority, not a question to answer alone.
examples: Do not touch her until the power is off; she is still standing in the water.
I have switched off the breaker and I am drying the floor and the pit now.
The pump is out of service until the electrician has checked the earth connection.
The installer certifies the installation, the owner keeps it, and the utility supplies the power.
sections.heading: After a shock in the water

item.summary: A pump moves water, and a pump that moves water can also move current. After reading this article you can name the parts of a pump installation, explain where the leakage comes from, say how current reaches a person through wet ground, compare the six protections that guard the circuit, run a safe check on a pump, and give the right instructions in the first minutes after a shock.
item.title: Water Pumps and the Risk of Electric Leakage
